sources.researchNote: The date is lettered on the print as 7-18-24. The view runs north from the Gansevoort Street market sheds along the Chelsea Piers, the line of piers from 54 to 62 to which the original Pier 57, built in 1907 and destroyed by fire in 1947, belonged. media.title: S.S. Champlain at Pier 57 — cabin-class salon, 1932
media.description: Cabin-class Salon de Thé aboard the French Line S.S. Champlain while associated with Pier 57 on the North River in 1932. The photograph documents the passenger-liner setting connected with the historical pier; it does not show the pier building or establish Kaper’s presence.
media.altText: Black-and-white photograph of the spacious cabin-class Salon de Thé aboard the S.S. Champlain, furnished with armchairs and small tables.
media.publicCaption: Cabin-class Salon de Thé aboard the French Line S.S. Champlain at Pier 57, North River, 1932.
media.publicCreditLine: Byron Company / Museum of the City of New York. 93.1.1.11445.
media.rightsNote: Copyright status has not been independently determined. The Museum of the City of New York describes conditions for non-commercial use of low-resolution images from its Collections Portal and notes that users must clear any copyright held by others. Its guidance requests a creator credit, accession number and link to the object record. The museum’s 2017 reproduction FAQ lists Byron Company among collections for which the museum can license images; it does not grant individual permission for this reproduction. The 800 × 614 local image is used for scholarly illustration of the passenger-liner context associated with Pier 57; the museum’s description of low resolution does not specify a pixel threshold for this image.

media.title: The North River piers at Chelsea from the air — U.S. Army Air Service photograph, 18 July 1924
media.description: Oblique aerial view northwards along the Hudson waterfront of Manhattan, taken by the 14th Photo Section of the U.S. Army Air Service and lettered on the print “118 Docks – New York Harbor, 7-18-24”. In the foreground are the market sheds at Gansevoort Street; north of them the long sheds of the Chelsea Piers line West Street, with liners at their berths, and Pennsylvania Station appears at the upper right. Pier 57, at the foot of West 15th Street, which the French Line used until 1936, is among the piers in the lower half of the picture; the photograph does not label the individual piers.
media.altText: Black-and-white aerial photograph of a row of long pier sheds projecting into a river, with ocean liners moored between them and a dense city grid stretching into the distance.
media.publicCaption: The Chelsea piers on the North River from the air, 18 July 1924. Pier 57, the French Line pier, is among those in the lower half of the picture.
media.publicCreditLine: 14th Photo Section, Air Service, U.S. Army; National Archives at College Park, Records of the Army Air Forces (RG 18), 18-AA-94-41, NAID 68146256.
media.rightsNote: Public domain. The photograph was taken by the U.S. Army Air Service in the course of official duties, so it is a work of the United States government and was never protected by copyright in the United States. The National Archives records no use restriction. The local copy is cropped to the photograph from the mounted print and reduced in size.

timelineEvents.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
timelineEvents.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper arrived in New York from France with Eleonora on a temporary visa, travelling onward to Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora sailed from Le Havre on 17 October 1934 aboard the S.S. Champlain in second cabin class and reached New York on 24 October. Their non-immigrant visas had been issued in Paris on 15 October, numbered in a single series with the Jurmanns’ (NI 1581–1584), and the manifest records Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as having paid the passage and as the party they were joining in Culver City. Kaper gave his occupation as musician and declared that he meant to stay about eight months and then return, without seeking United States citizenship. David Blum of the Culver Export Corporation met them in New York, and they left for Hollywood on 27 October.

places.authorizedName: French Line Pier 57, North River, foot of West 15th Street, Manhattan, New York
places.publicNote: Approximate arrival site for Kaper and Eleonora’s 1934 Atlantic crossing from Le Havre aboard the S.S. Champlain. In this period the French Line (Compagnie Générale Transatlantique) used Pier 57 on the North River, at the foot of West 15th Street; the pier is inferred from the line’s documented berth rather than named in the passenger manifest. The record establishes arrival at New York but not processing at Ellis Island.
